title: Social Sciences Exclusion
description: The social sciences exclusion, IRC § 41(d)(4)(G), bars R&D credit claims for research in the social sciences, arts or humanities.
summary: The social sciences exclusion is a federal R&D tax credit rule under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8) that bars U.S. taxpayers from claiming qualified research expenses for research in the social sciences (including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences), arts, or humanities. The key takeaway: the research process, not the end result, determines eligibility.

body.text: The social sciences exclusion is a federal R&D tax credit rule under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8) that bars U.S. taxpayers from claiming qualified research expenses for research in the social sciences (including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences), arts, or humanities. The key takeaway: the research process, not the end result, determines eligibility.
Executive Summary and Statutory Mandate

The Social Sciences Exclusion (SSE) establishes a bright-line statutory boundary on the definition of "qualified research" eligible for the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit—formally titled the Credit for Increasing Research Activities—under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41). Codified at IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and elaborated under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8) (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(8), which succeeded the pre-1986 regulatory framework codified at Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(c), formerly designated as § 1.41-5(c) prior to Treasury Decision 8930), the exclusion bars systematic investigations conducted within the social sciences, arts, or humanities from generating Qualified Research Expenses (QREs). Both the implementing regulations at Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8) and administrative guidance in the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Audit Techniques Guides (ATGs) explicitly define the excluded social sciences domain to encompass economics, business management, and behavioral sciences, alongside the arts and humanities.

Functioning as a mandatory negative filter within IRC § 41(d)(4), the SSE disqualifies corporate initiatives that employ structured empirical methodologies to address non-technical objectives. Activities such as designing novel employee compensation frameworks, restructuring manufacturing organizations, developing new life insurance contracts or accounting procedures, modeling macroeconomic trends to inform corporate strategy, and administering consumer preference surveys are ineligible for the research tax credit regardless of their analytical rigor or empirical sophistication. Through this statutory prohibition, the legislative and regulatory framework confines the federal R&D tax subsidy to the resolution of technical uncertainty rooted in the physical sciences, biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

From a fiscal policy standpoint, the SSE preserves the structural integrity of IRC § 41 by reinforcing the "Technological in Nature" requirement of the statutory four-part test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(4). The federal R&D tax credit was enacted to correct market failures by incentivizing technical experimentation in disciplines where social returns substantially exceed private returns—an economic dynamic characteristic of applied engineering and fundamental physical or laboratory sciences rather than routine commercial, financial, or organizational optimization. Within the broader statutory architecture of IRC § 41(d)(4), the SSE pairs with parallel exclusions under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(5) for "Surveys, studies, etc." and activities relating to management functions or techniques, alongside IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) excluding style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors, thereby removing both the academic disciplines of the social sciences and their primary data-gathering methodologies from credit eligibility.

In contemporary corporate environments where software engineering, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), data analytics, and human-computer interaction (HCI) converge, the SSE imposes strict cost-segregation and substantiation obligations under IRC § 6001 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d). Taxpayers operating in hybrid technological domains must isolate disqualified behavioral, sociological, or economic research expenditures—such as psychological user-interface (UI) framing studies or employee retention trend analyses—from qualified computer science expenditures—such as core algorithmic latency optimization or distributed database architecture design—to satisfy the "substantially all" (80 percent) threshold of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and withstand IRS examination scrutiny.
Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of IRC Section 41
The Four-Part Qualification Test and Hard Science Reliance

Eligibility for the federal research tax credit under IRC § 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(2) requires that a claimed research activity satisfy a cumulative four-part statutory test—applied separately to each discrete business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A)—governing its underlying expenditure deductibility and permitted purpose, elimination of technical uncertainty, scientific foundation, and experimental methodology. Even where an activity appears to satisfy elements of this affirmative test, IRC § 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(1) mandate that "qualified research" does not include any activity described in the exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) or IRC § 41(d)(4). Failure to satisfy any single affirmative prong, or falling within an enumerated statutory exclusion such as the SSE under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G), results in the disallowance of the associated expenditures for that activity.

A rigorous, hypothesis-driven empirical methodology cannot cure a subject-matter defect if the hypotheses tested are grounded in excluded soft sciences rather than principles of physical or biological science, engineering, or computer science.
Explicitly excludes all research conducted in the social sciences (expressly including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences), arts, or humanities.

Operates as an overriding statutory veto that supersedes preliminary compliance with systematic empirical evaluation and business-component improvement tests, barring SSE costs even from the 20% non-experimentation allowance under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6).

body.text: The "Technological in Nature" prong under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(4) establishes the conceptual baseline against which the SSE operates. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover such information "fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science" (though a taxpayer may employ existing technologies and rely on existing principles within those four disciplines to satisfy this requirement, and need not seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field under § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii)). This four-discipline formulation builds upon the pre-1986 regulatory standard in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(c), which contrasted excluded social sciences and humanities against "research in a field of laboratory science (such as physics or biochemistry), engineering or technology". Within the four statutory pillars of physical sciences, biological sciences, engineering, and computer science, applied sub-disciplines—including chemistry, physics, and astronomy within the physical sciences, or biochemistry and food science (illustrated in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 3, involving food-product manufacturing line modifications) within the biological and engineering sciences—qualify when experimentation relies fundamentally on their scientific principles.

The SSE delineates the negative boundary of the "Technological in Nature" requirement by confirming that theories derived from human behavior, market dynamics, actuarial or financial forecasting, artistic expression, historical inquiry, or organizational administration lie outside the statutory definition of technology. In TSR, Inc. v. Commissioner, 96 T.C. 903 (1991), the United States Tax Court examined the legislative history of the research credit and the scope of the social sciences and humanities exclusion, concluding that statutory "research" is limited to scientific and laboratory experimentation in the technological sense rather than gathering literary, historical, or game-development information. Similarly, in United Stationers, Inc. v. United States (7th Cir., affirming 982 F. Supp. 1279 (N.D. Ill. 1997)), the court emphasized that uncertainty regarding the aspired commercial or operational benefits of a software project does not constitute technical uncertainty when the development of the technological means to achieve those benefits is not in doubt. Consequently, an activity that systematically tests hypotheses to improve a business component still fails the statutory standard if its investigative mechanism relies on behavioral modeling, sociological analysis, or economic forecasting rather than hard scientific principles.
Positioning Within the Statutory Exclusions of IRC Section 41(d)(4)

Within the internal structure of IRC § 41(d)(4) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c), the SSE operates alongside seven adjacent statutory exclusions—forming eight excluded categories in total—designed to strip standard commercial lifecycle, administrative, and non-technological activities from the R&D tax credit base. Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A)–(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)–(9), qualified research excludes: (1) research conducted after the beginning of commercial production (IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)), including preproduction planning, tooling up, accumulating data relating to production processes, debugging flaws, and routine quality control; (2) adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need (IRC § 41(d)(4)(B), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3)); (3) duplication or reproduction of an existing business component from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information (IRC § 41(d)(4)(C), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(4)); (4) efficiency surveys, activities relating to management functions or techniques, market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), routine data collections, and routine testing or inspection for quality control (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(5)); (5) research with respect to computer software developed by or for the benefit of the taxpayer primarily for internal use in general and administrative functions, unless it satisfies a statutory exception or the three-part "high threshold of innovation" test (IRC § 41(d)(4)(E), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)); (6) foreign research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States (IRC § 41(d)(4)(F), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(7), § 1.41-4A(b)); (7) any research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities (IRC § 41(d)(4)(G), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8), § 1.41-4A(c)); and (8) research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9), § 1.41-4A(d)). Additionally, under the threshold IRC § 174 test incorporated by IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(6)(vii) excludes research in connection with literary, historical, or similar projects involving the production of films, sound recordings, video tapes, books, or similar properties.

This statutory placement confirms that the SSE functions as an overriding subject-matter veto. Even where a corporate taxpayer designs a controlled empirical study to evaluate the correlation between organizational hierarchy and net profitability—thereby addressing methodological uncertainty through systematic data analysis—the expenditure is immediately disqualified because business management and economics are enumerated as excluded disciplines under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8), as well as under the management-functions exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(5)(ii). Furthermore, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(7) ("Use of computers and information technology") explicitly mandates that the employment of computers or information technology, or reliance on principles of computer science or information technology to store, collect, manipulate, translate, disseminate, produce, distribute, or process data or information, does not itself establish that qualified research has been undertaken. Deploying advanced statistical software, machine learning packages, or computational measurement instruments to conduct a management, behavioral, or economic study does not convert the underlying social science inquiry into qualified technological research.
Regulatory Interpretation and the Process-Over-Result Doctrine
Scope of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(8)

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8)—applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, pursuant to Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(e)—governs the administrative application of the SSE by providing verbatim: "Qualified research does not include research in the social sciences (including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences), arts, or humanities.". Its predecessor provision governing taxable years beginning before January 1, 1986 (and cross-referenced for basic research under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-5A(e)(2)), Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(c), similarly explains that the phrase "research in the social sciences or humanities" encompasses all areas of research other than research in a field of laboratory science (such as physics or biochemistry), engineering, or technology, and provides explicit examples of disqualified activities: "the development of a new life insurance contract, a new economic model or theory, a new accounting procedure or a new cookbook.". In corporate practice, the regulatory inclusion of economics and business management eliminates tax credit claims for operational efficiency restructurings, actuarial or financial product modeling, new accounting procedures, and quantitative marketing models engineered around macroeconomic or consumer demand forecasting.

Simultaneously, the regulatory prohibition on "behavioral sciences" under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8) creates acute compliance friction in contemporary software, digital platform, and AI development. As digital platforms increasingly integrate human-computer interaction (HCI), behavioral nudges, and personalized algorithmic feeds, product development teams routinely combine computational engineering with psychological user testing. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8), read in conjunction with the uncertainty and technological-in-nature standards of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4) and the aesthetic/taste exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), whenever the primary uncertainty under investigation concerns human behavior, cognitive response, aesthetic preference, or consumer choice—rather than the technical capability, method, or engineering design of the underlying software or hardware architecture—the SSE bars the expenditure.
The Governing Principle: Process Versus Ultimate Benefit

A foundational interpretive rule emphasized in the IRS Audit Techniques Guides (Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 - Qualified Research Activities, Section 7, "Exclusion for research in the social sciences, etc.") is that the process of experimentation—rather than the commercial context, functional application, or end result of the research—determines qualification under the SSE. As the IRS Audit Techniques Guide states explicitly: "Note that the process, not the end result, governs. The development of new formulation of artists' paint would not be excluded simply because it benefited the arts, while research into Van Gogh's life would be excluded under this rule.". This process-over-result doctrine protects taxpayers whose hard-science engineering produces a business component destined for use within an excluded field.

For example, the systematic development of a novel chemical formulation for specialized artists' paint qualifies for the R&D tax credit because the experimental process relies fundamentally on principles of chemistry and material science (physical sciences and engineering under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(4)) to resolve technical uncertainty regarding pigment stability or viscosity. Although the finished product directly benefits and serves the arts—an explicitly excluded domain under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8)—the research process itself is technological in nature. Conversely, a systematic historical investigation into the life and painting techniques of Vincent van Gogh is disqualified under the SSE because the investigative process lies entirely within the humanities. Eligibility thus hinges on whether the taxpayer incurred expenses to resolve technical uncertainty through hard-science principles, irrespective of whether the resulting product operates within an artistic, economic, behavioral, or managerial environment.
Intersection with Parallel Exclusions and Regulatory Precedent

The operational reach of the SSE is reinforced by its overlap with the statutory exclusions for "Surveys, studies, etc." and management functions under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(5). While the SSE under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8) disqualifies the overarching academic and professional disciplines of sociology, psychology, economics, and business management, the surveys-and-studies exclusion under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(5)(i)–(v) targets the specific empirical methodologies—efficiency surveys ((c)(5)(i)), management functions or techniques including preparation of financial data and analysis, development of employee training programs and management organization plans, and management-based changes in production processes such as rearranging workstations on an assembly line ((c)(5)(ii)), market research, testing, or development including advertising or promotions ((c)(5)(iii)), routine data collections ((c)(5)(iv)), and routine or ordinary testing or inspections for quality control ((c)(5)(v))—commonly utilized by those disciplines. Similarly, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 1 illustrates that surveying customers to determine which shade of green paint customers prefer for a widget is not qualified research because the activities relate to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii).

In enforcing these boundaries, IRS examination teams and both the general IRS Research Credit ATG and the IRS Software ATG (Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software) consistently rely on the regulatory illustrations codified at Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 9 and Example 10 (note that while general commentary occasionally miscites Example 10 as § 1.41-4(c)(8), Example 10, all exclusion examples in § 1.41-4(c) are codified in subparagraph (c)(10), "Illustrations"). In Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 9, taxpayer X, a manufacturing corporation, undertakes to restructure its manufacturing organization and organizes a team—including X's employees as well as outside management consultants—to design an organizational structure that will improve X's business operations; the regulation concludes that X's activities are excluded because qualified research does not include activities relating to management functions or techniques, including management organization plans and management-based changes in production processes under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(5). In Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 10, taxpayer X, an insurance company, develops a new life insurance product and, in the course of developing the product, engages in research with respect to the effect of pricing and tax consequences on demand for the product, the expected volatility of interest rates, and the expected mortality rates (based on published data). Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 10 holds that X's activities related to the new product represent research in the social sciences (including economics and business management) and are thus excluded from the definition of qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8).

Furthermore, historical administrative rulemaking from the January 2, 2004 Federal Register cycle—specifically Treasury Decision 9104 (T.D. 9104, RIN 1545-AY82, 69 FR 22–29, published January 2, 2004, under Federal Register Document Number 03-31818), which promulgated the final regulations under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4 (including § 1.41-4(c)(8) and § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 10), and the companion Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (REG-153656-03, RIN 1545-BC70, Announcement 2004-9, 69 FR 43–46, published January 2, 2004, under Federal Register Document Number 03-31819), which invited public comments on internal-use software under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and was later withdrawn and replaced by the 2015 proposed regulations (80 FR 2622, Jan. 20, 2015, Document 2015-00690) and the October 4, 2016 Final Regulations (T.D. 9786, 2016-42 I.R.B.)—reflects earlier industrial, financial, and software models that predated the modern convergence of deep learning, behavioral analytics, and HCI.
Practical Application and Cost Segregation in Hybrid R&D
Hypothetical Case Study 1: FinTech Platform Development (AlphaTech)

The compliance complexities surrounding the SSE are most pronounced in financial technology (FinTech), artificial intelligence, and data analytics, where product engineering teams operate alongside behavioral economists. A hypothetical scenario involving a FinTech enterprise ("AlphaTech") demonstrates how the SSE mandates granular activity and cost bifurcation within a single product launch. Suppose AlphaTech undertakes the development of a proprietary online investment platform that deploys machine learning (ML) models to generate personalized equity recommendations for retail users through two concurrent workstreams.

In the first workstream, addressing behavioral science and business management, AlphaTech's product and behavioral research team conducts structured A/B testing on the platform's user interface (UI). The team systematically tests variations in prompt sequencing, the spatial placement of investment execution buttons, and psychological framing anchors (including color psychology and loss-aversion phrasing) to maximize the user's propensity to click "invest now". Although the team follows a rigorous, data-driven experimental protocol, the core uncertainty being resolved is how to influence human financial behavior to increase commercial conversion rates. Because this activity relies fundamentally on behavioral economics and marketing psychology rather than principles of computer science or engineering, it falls squarely within the SSE under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8), as well as the market research and style/taste exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(5)(iii)) and IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii) and (a)(8), Example 1). Moreover, under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(7), using software analytics tools to collect and process A/B clickstream data does not make the behavioral study technological in nature. All associated wages and overhead incurred by researchers conducting the UI psychological analysis are therefore ineligible for the R&D tax credit.

In the concurrent second workstream, centered on computer science and network engineering, AlphaTech's software engineering team designs a novel, proprietary database architecture capable of ingesting, normalizing, and aggregating 50 distinct real-time market data feeds so that the ML inference engine can deliver personalized stock recommendations within a strict 200-millisecond (200 ms) latency threshold. At the outset of development, the engineering team faces technical uncertainty under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3) regarding whether the proposed distributed data architecture can sustain the required throughput and sub-200 ms latency under peak market volume. The engineers conduct systematic hypothesis testing and algorithmic benchmarking using principles of computer science and network engineering (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4)–(5)). Furthermore, because the platform is developed to enable the taxpayer to interact with third parties and allow retail users to initiate investment functions and review data on AlphaTech's system, it is not treated as general and administrative internal-use software under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv). Even though the commercial output of the platform facilitates economic investment decisions, the research process resolves a pure technical uncertainty via hard science. Consequently, this engineering workstream satisfies the "Technological in Nature" test, avoids the SSE under the process-over-result doctrine, and generates eligible QREs for engineering wages and computing supplies.
Hypothetical Case Study 2: AI Human-Resources Tool ("Retention Bot") Cost Allocation

The total project budget is $500,000, distributed across four discrete project tasks that blend technical software engineering ($300,000 combined across Tasks 1 and 3) with psychological and sociological profiling ($200,000 combined across Tasks 2 and 4).

body.text: Recomputing the project cost allocation step-by-step confirms the exact financial impact of the exclusion:

items: Compliant QRE Pool: Task 1 Expenditures (Design Database Schema) + Task 3 Expenditures (Algorithm Coding in Python) = $300,000.
Excluded SSE Amount: Task 2 Expenditures (Employee Survey Design) + Task 4 Expenditures (Analyze Retention Trends) = $200,000.
Compliant QRE Ratio: $300,000 / $500,000 = 60% (with the remaining $200,000 / $500,000 = 40% excluded under the SSE).

body.text: If the taxpayer files an aggressive claim that bundles all four tasks ($300,000 in eligible hard-science expenses combined with $200,000 in ineligible social-science expenses for a $500,000 QRE claim), the inclusion of psychological employee survey design (Task 2) and sociological/managerial retention trend analysis (Task 4) triggers severe IRS audit exposure under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and (D). Specifically, under the "substantially all" rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6), even where 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation, the remaining 20 percent or less is eligible only "so long as these remaining research activities satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1)(A) and are not otherwise excluded under section 41(d)(4)". Because Tasks 2 and 4 are excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and (D), they can never be included in QREs. Furthermore, if the taxpayer fails to segregate the software engineering subcomponents (Tasks 1 and 3) from the soft-science tasks (Tasks 2 and 4) via the shrinking-back rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2), the qualified experimentation activities ($300,000) would represent only 60 percent of the $500,000 aggregate project—failing the 80 percent "substantially all" threshold of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6) for the overall project. Conversely, a compliant claim applies IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) to isolate the software engineering wages incurred to build the database schema and Python algorithm, restricting the QRE pool to $300,000 (60% of total project spend) and reducing soft-science audit exposure to $0. (If "Retention Bot" is developed primarily for the taxpayer's internal personnel management use rather than for commercial sale or licensing to third parties, Tasks 1 and 3 must also satisfy the three-part "high threshold of innovation" test for internal-use software under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii).)
Compliance Imperatives and Audit Risk Mitigation

During IRS examinations of R&D tax credit claims—particularly in software, marketing technology (MarTech), educational technology (EdTech), and management consulting—auditors utilize the IRS Research Credit ATG and the Software Process of Experimentation Audit Guidelines to scrutinize whether claimed experimentation relies fundamentally on hard sciences. When taxpayers bundle focus group expenditures, market viability studies, consumer survey design, actuarial demand modeling, or management consulting fees into engineering cost centers, examination teams invoke IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) and (c)(10), Example 10) and the parallel exclusions under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(5) and (c)(10), Example 9) to disallow the contaminated cost pools.

To mitigate audit risk in hybrid projects where computer science and behavioral analysis intersect, corporate taxpayers must implement three structural compliance controls derived from the regulatory framework under IRC § 6001 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)–(d):

items: Granular Cost-Center and Payroll Segregation: Accounting systems must establish distinct project codes and business-component sub-ledgers (IRC § 41(d)(2)(A), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)) that separate technical development from content, behavioral, or market research. Time-tracking protocols must ensure that wages paid to economists, behavioral scientists, management consultants, or UX psychologists testing feature effectiveness are excluded, while wages paid to software engineers developing the underlying computational architecture required to deliver that feature are captured separately, preventing excluded soft-science hours from diluting the 80 percent "substantially all" test (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)) or contaminating the 80 percent wage rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)).

Precision in Contemporaneous Technical Narratives: Under IRC § 6001 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d), contemporaneous documentation must explicitly articulate how experimentation relied on computer science, engineering, or physical/biological science principles (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4)) to resolve technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or design (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)). Where a software project incorporates economic or behavioral theories, the project narrative should expressly state that while the application utilizes economic or behavioral models, the uncertainty resolved by the engineering team was strictly technical—such as database throughput or algorithmic latency—rather than an investigation into the validity of the economic, actuarial, or psychological theory itself.

Strict Tool-Versus-Content Differentiation: Internal compliance reviews must apply a strict tool-versus-content differentiation when evaluating the process of experimentation under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5) and (a)(7) alongside the IRS ATG process-over-result doctrine, distinguishing between the technological tool being engineered (which is eligible if it resolves hard-science uncertainty) and the behavioral, sociological, or economic content that the tool processes or measures (which is excluded under the SSE and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(7)). Research aimed at developing or optimizing the technical algorithm, architecture, or hardware used to measure, track, or model behavior qualifies; conversely, research aimed at interpreting user behavior findings or selecting optimal marketing or organizational interventions must be excluded.

body.text: Policy Recommendations for Regulatory Modernization
Issuance of Updated Treasury Guidance Addressing AI and HCI Overlap

The Department of the Treasury and the IRS should publish updated proposed regulations or formal administrative notices expanding upon Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 10 (which currently illustrates only traditional life insurance product development involving pricing, tax consequences, interest rate volatility, and mortality rates). Updated regulatory examples under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(10) should establish granular, fact-intensive standards distinguishing qualified computer science research—such as natural language processing (NLP) algorithm design, deep learning model optimization, and computational methods for processing massive datasets—from excluded behavioral science activities—such as UX preference studies, psychological engagement testing, and sociological modeling for commercial prediction. Providing explicit cost-segregation examples within a single AI project (for instance, contrasting algorithmic latency reduction in a recommendation engine against psychological research into which recommendation content maximizes user engagement) would substantially reduce examination disputes.
Refining the Regulatory Definition of Behavioral Sciences in Technical Contexts

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(8) should be amended—or cross-referenced with Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(4) and (a)(7)—to clarify that the "behavioral sciences" exclusion applies only where research is intended to resolve uncertainty regarding human preference, organizational structure, or macroeconomic conditions without the concurrent resolution of technical uncertainty in the capability, method, or design of the underlying technological component. The revised regulation should affirmatively state that utilizing computer science, mathematics, or engineering to measure, track, or model human behavior is not automatically disqualified by the SSE, provided the primary objective of the activity is the technical development or improvement of the computational measurement or modeling tool itself. This refinement would codify the IRS ATG "process over result" principle within hybrid AI and behavioral-analytics environments.
Interagency Harmonization of Federal Research Definitions

Aligning tax administration with NSF and NIST scientific definitions would clarify that fundamental computational, mathematical, and engineering research remains eligible for the R&D tax credit even when applied to complex behavioral datasets, fulfilling the legislative objective of stimulating technical innovation with high social returns.
